passage:
Vishal, beta, sit. You think your Nani was born typing fast? At twenty I was at the Sharma Commercial Institute learning shorthand, and I was stuck at eighty words a minute for a whole winter. Every evening I took dictation from the radio news, page after page, and every evening the same outlines tangled me: the long words, the numbers.
One day I stopped doing whole pages. I made a list of only the outlines I kept missing, forty or so, and wrote each one slowly, ten times, with nothing else on the desk. No radio, no chatting with the other girls. Then I took my notebook to Kamla-ji, the senior stenographer in the court, and asked her to mark my mistakes. She circled things I hadn't even noticed.
Three weeks, beta. I crossed a hundred by Holi.

qa.q: What speed was Nani stuck at for a whole winter?
qa.a: She was stuck at eighty words a minute for a whole winter.

qa.q: Why might Nani have been feeling discouraged before she changed her practice?
qa.a: She was working hard every evening, page after page, yet the same outlines kept tangling her, so her effort seemed wasted.

qa.q: Which change in Nani's practice made the difference, and why?
qa.a: She listed only the outlines she kept missing, wrote them slowly with full attention, and asked Kamla-ji to mark her mistakes; targeted work fixed the weak spots that whole pages hid.

qa.q: What might Vishal take from hearing this story from his Nani?
qa.a: Vishal may see that being stuck is normal and that changing how you practise, not just adding hours, is what moves you forward.

grounding: It shows a young learner isolating the weak part, slowing down, getting feedback from someone more skilled and practising with full attention.

The hostel warden locked the terrace at nine, which left Yamini exactly twenty minutes of flute in the back stairwell after dinner. Her roommate's exams had begun, so the room was out.
For a month she had spent those twenty minutes playing the whole Hamsadhwani piece from the top, and the same fast passage in the middle fell apart every time.
On Monday she tried something different. She played only those six notes, slowly, with a metronome ticking on her phone, until they came out even. Then one notch faster. Nothing else. Twenty minutes felt long for six notes.
On Thursday she sent a recording to Ramesh, the senior who led the music club. His reply came back in an hour: 'You're running out of breath before the run. Breathe two notes earlier.' She had never noticed.
By the next weekend the passage held together.

qa.q: Where did Yamini practise after dinner?
qa.a: Yamini practised in the back stairwell after dinner.

qa.q: How do you think Yamini felt reading Ramesh's reply?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and relieved, because he spotted a breathing problem she had never noticed herself.

qa.q: What made Yamini's twenty minutes work better than a month of full run-throughs?
qa.a: She isolated the six hard notes, slowed them down with a metronome, and asked someone better for feedback, so every minute went to the weak spot.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel about being asked for feedback?
qa.a: Ramesh may feel trusted and glad to help, and the specific recording made it easy for him to spot the real problem.

grounding: It shows a learner with little time isolating the weak passage, slowing it down, seeking feedback from a stronger player and practising attentively.
